activities.title: Deconstructing Your First Java Program
activities.content:
### The Anatomy of Hello World
Every single line in a Java program has a specific purpose. Here is the canonical starter program:

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, LearnBySelf!");
    }
}
```

Let us break it down piece by piece:

#### 1. `public class Main`
In Java, **all code must live inside a class**. A class is a container or blueprint for code.
* `public`: Means this class can be accessed by anyone, including the JVM from the outside.
* `class`: The keyword used to declare a Java class.
* `Main`: The name of the class. **Rule of Gold**: If a class is declared `public`, its file name must match exactly including capitalization (`Main.java`).

#### 2. `public static void main(String[] args)`
This is the designated entry point for every standalone Java program:
* `public`: Visible to the JVM so it can launch the program.
* `static`: Allows the JVM to call this method directly on the class **without creating an object first**. This is critical: when your program first boots up, no objects exist in memory yet! If `main` were not static, Java would be stuck in a chicken-and-egg dilemma.
* `void`: The return type. It means this method finishes its work and returns nothing back to the operating system.
* `main`: The method name the JVM specifically looks for.
* `String[] args`: An array of text strings representing command-line arguments passed to the program when launched.

#### 3. `System.out.println(...)`
* `System`: A built-in class provided by Java containing system-level utilities.
* `out`: The standard output stream (connected to your terminal/console).
* `println`: Short for 'print line'. It outputs the text enclosed in quotes and automatically moves the cursor to a new line. In contrast, `System.out.print` prints text without adding a newline.

breakdown.whatIsIt: A Java program is a structured file containing a class and a standard main method entry point that outputs to the console.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Understanding each keyword prevents common compile errors and prepares you to write clean, modular software.
howItWorks: 1. JVM boots up and loads the class into memory
2. JVM locates public static void main(String[] args)
3. Statements inside the curly braces execute line by line from top to bottom
keyTakeaways: Filename must match public class name (Main.java)
main() must be static so the JVM can run it without creating an instance
println adds a newline after printing; print does not

activities.title: Printing Formatted Multi-Line Output
activities.description: Each call to System.out.println prints its argument to the terminal and inserts a newline. Note the closing semicolon (;) at the end of each statement.

questions.question: Why is the main method declared 'static' in Java?
options: So that its variables cannot be modified by other methods.
So the JVM can invoke it directly without having to instantiate an object of the class first.
Because Java does not support non-static methods.
To make the program run faster by skipping memory allocation.
questions.explanation: When a program starts, no objects exist yet. Making main static allows the JVM to invoke Main.main() directly on the class blueprint.
hints: Think about what exists in memory at the exact moment a program launches.

questions.question: If your file contains 'public class StudentRecord', what MUST the file name on disk be?
options: Any name is acceptable as long as it ends in .java
questions.explanation: In Java, a public class must reside in a file that matches its exact name and casing, followed by the .java extension.
hints: Java is strictly case-sensitive: StudentRecord requires StudentRecord.java.

questions.question: What is the difference between System.out.print() and System.out.println()?
options: System.out.print can only print numbers, while println prints text.
System.out.println prints the content and then appends a newline, whereas print leaves the cursor on the same line.
There is no difference; they are aliases for each other.
System.out.println sends output to a printer instead of the screen.

interviewQA.question: What happens if you remove the 'static' keyword from the main method in Java?
interviewQA.answer: The program will compile cleanly with javac without errors, because syntactically a method can be non-static. However, when you attempt to run it with 'java Main', the JVM will throw a runtime error: 'Main method is not static in class Main, please define the main method as: public static void main(String[] args)'. The JVM explicitly looks for a static method signature.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Missing 'static' in main is a runtime error, not a compile-time error.

interviewQA.question: Can a single .java source file have multiple classes? What are the rules?
interviewQA.answer: Yes, a single Java file can contain multiple classes. However, at most ONE class can be declared 'public', and the file name must match that public class name. If there are other classes in the file, they must have default (package-private) access. When compiled, javac will produce a separate .class file for every class declared in that file.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: At most one public class per file, matching the filename. javac generates a .class file for each class.
